parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek -ῐκός (-ĭkós) or Latin -icus.

parole.significato: absorption (act or process of absorbing or sucking in anything)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Absorption, or French absorption, from Latin absorptiō. First attested in 1825.

parole.significato: advocate, attorney, barrister, solicitor, lawyer, counsel
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin advocātus. Etymology 1, noun sense 2 is a semantic loan from German Advokat and French avocat. First attested in 1559.

parole.significato: agitation, agitprop, campaigning (spreading of ideals and values in the goal of gaining more followers)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Agitation or from French agitation, from Latin agitātiō. First attested in 1661.

parole.significato: to agitate, to doorstep, to campaign (to convince to adopt certain views) [with accusative ‘whom’] or [with wśród (+ ge…
parole.testo: Internationalism; compare English agitate. Possibly borrowed from German agitieren or from French agiter, ultimately from Latin āgitō + -ować. First attested in 1616.

parole.significato: agglomerate (something clumped together from different substances)
parole.testo: Internationalism; compare English agglomerate. Possibly borrowed from French agglomérat or from German Agglomerat, ultimately from Latin agglomerō + -at. First attested in 1833.
Internationalism; compare English agglomerate. Possibly borrowed from German agglomerieren or from French agglomérer, ultimately Latin agglomerō + -ować. First attested in 1848.

Internationalism; compare English agony. Possible borrowed from German Agonie or from French agonie, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía, “emulation, competition, struggle”), from ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”). First attested in 1722.

parole.significato: academic, member of an academy (member of an institution or building for the study of higher learning)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin acadēmicus. Etymology 2 sense 2, etymology 2 sense 4 and etymology 2 sense 5 are semantic loans from German Akademiker and French académicien. First attested in 1577.

parole.significato: action, mission, campaign, operation (something done in order to accomplish something)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin āctiō (“act of doing or making”). Noun sense 1 and noun sense 6 are semantic loans from German Aktion or French action. First attested in 1553.
Learned borrowing from Latin āctus. Etymology 1 sense 5 is a semantic loan from German Akt. First attested in 1529.

parole.significato: album (book specially designed to keep photographs, stamps, or autographs)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Album or French album. First attested in 1609.

parole.significato: anatomy (science that deals with the form and structure of organic bodies)
parole.testo: Internationalism; possibly borrowed from German Anatomie, or French anatomie, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “dissection”). By surface analysis, ana- + -tomia. First attested in the 16th century.

parole.significato: fingering (a specific method of using the fingers to play an instrument)
parole.testo: From either German Apllikatur or Italian applicatura.
From either French aposiopèse or English aposiopesis, from Ancient Greek ἀποσιώπησις (aposiṓpēsis).
From either French aposiopèse or English aposiopesis, from Ancient Greek ἀποσιώπησις (aposiṓpēsis).
From either Latin arcātūra or French arcature.

parole.significato: harlequinade (a pantomime-like comedy featuring the harlequin or clown)
parole.testo: From either French arlequinade or Italian arlecchinata. By surface analysis, arlekin + -ada.
Either borrowed from French attentat or borrowed from German Attentat.

parole.significato: attraction (event, location, or business that has a tendency to draw interest from visitors, and in many cases, local r…
parole.testo: Either borrowed from French attraction or German Attraktion, from Old French attraction, from Latin attractiō.

parole.significato: to lamb (to give birth to a baby sheep)
parole.testo: Back-formation of Proto-Slavic *o(b)- + *agniti. Compare Slovincian bagnjic sã.

parole.significato: banishment, exile (punishment of being forbidden to enter one's home country or city, usually under penalty of death)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin bannitio, or from banita + -cja, from Old French banir, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną.

parole.significato: launch (the boat of the largest size and/or of most importance belonging to a ship of war)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish barcaza, or from French barcasse.
Possibly borrowed from Italian basso, or from French basse or German Bass, ultimately from Latin bassus. Compare Slovincian bas.
Borrowed from Swedish bat or Italian batto.

parole.significato: barrel (round vessel made from staves bound with a hoop)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish beczka. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English barrel roll, French tonneau, and German Fassrolle.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bělъkъ. By surface analysis, biały + -ko. Noun sense 2 is a semantic loan from Latin albūmen. For noun sense 4, compare English white (of the eye) and German weiße (Augenhaut).

parole.significato: current (existing or occurring at the moment)
parole.testo: From bieżeć + -ący. Adjective sense 1 is a semantic loan from German laufend, French courant, and English current. First attested in 1500–1547.
Unadapted borrowing from English boss, from Dutch baas, from Middle Dutch baes, from Old Dutch *baso, from Proto-Germanic *baswô.
Borrowed from French broche, from Old French broche, from Vulgar Latin *brocca, from either Ancient Greek πρόχοος (prókhoos) or βροχίς (brokhís), with influence from broccus.
Either from German Bolle or Latin bulbus.
Inherited from Old Polish byk. Sense 5 is a semantic loan from English bull market. Sense 6 is a semantic loan from English bull.
Inherited from Old Polish bóbr. Sense 3 is a semantic loan from English beaver
Borrowed from French benjoin or from Italian benzoino. Doublet of benzoes and benzoina.
Borrowed from Belarusian благі́ (blahí) or Ukrainian благи́й (blahýj). Doublet of błogi (“blissful”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; modificatore <unc> nel legame; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *xȗjь. This word in noun 1 sense 1 was not attested until 1806 (however, Wacław Potocki of Łużna [Lesser Poland] used it in his texts from 1669 and 1677), and was only an urban word. For this reason, Sławski considered the word to be a borrowing from Old Ruthe
Borrowed from Russian хват (xvat) and/or Ukrainian хват (xvat). Related to chwacić, chwatać, chwytać.

parole.significato: body (physical structure of a human or animal seen as one single organism)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish ciało. Sense 5 is a semantic loan from Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma) and Latin corpus. Sense 6 is a semantic loan from Latin corpus. Sense 7 is a semantic loan from French corps.

parole.significato: bitch (inmate used as a sexual object)
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from German Schwelle or from German schwul.

Mazurized form of *czyga, likely borrowed, but the exact language is sometimes disputed. Some point to Hungarian csiga (“snail”); compare csigalépcső where the same word means "spiral" as the first element. Alternatively, borrowed from Slovak čiga. However, Bańkowski disputes Hungarian origin, and a

Borrowed from French début, from Middle French, derivative of desbuter (“to move, begin”), from des- + but (“mark, goal”), from Old French but (“aim, goal, end, target”), either from Old French butte (“mound, knoll, target”), from Frankish *but (“stump, log”), or from Old Norse bútr (“log, stump, bu
Borrowed from German Doppelschnepfe and French double-bécassine.

parole.significato: director (person in charge of a directorate)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dīrēctor. Noun 1 sense 1 and noun 1 sense 2 are semantic loans from German Direktor and French directeur.

parole.significato: operation (activity undertaken by someone for a specific purpose)
parole.testo: From działalny + -ość. Sense 1 is a semantic loan from German Tätigkeit and French activité. First attested in 1802.
From dzień + -nik. Originally, a calque of Latin diārium, later senses are a semantic loan from French journal. First attested in 1532.
From dzięka + -i, which was also displaced by this term. Compare Czech díky. Preposition sense 1 is a semantic loan from German dank, French grâce à, and English thanks to.
Borrowed from English evaluation and/or from French évaluation.

parole.significato: synonym of rodzina (“family”) (husband and wife and their children)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin familia. Sense 6 is a semantic loan from Russian фами́лия (famílija). First attested in 1559.
Learned borrowing from Latin fundus. Sense 3 is a semantic loan from French fonds. First attested in 1543. Compare Silesian fōndusz.

Borrowed from English game, from Middle English game, gamen, gammen, from Old English gamen (“sport, joy, mirth, pastime, game, amusement, pleasure”), from Proto-West Germanic *gaman, from Proto-Germanic *gamaną (“amusement, pleasure, game”), from *ga- (collective prefix) + *mann- (“man”); or altern

parole.significato: talon, claw (sharp, hooked claw of a bird of prey or other predatory animal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French griffe (“talon”), from Middle French griffe, either deverbal from griffer, which see, or through an unattested Old French noun from Old High German grif, from Proto-Germanic *gripiz, which would make it a doublet of gryf (“grip”). First attested in 1807.
Deverbal from grypsnąć (“to snatch”), from German gripsen. Alternatively, borrowed from German Grips (“wit”).
Borrowed from German Halle or French halle. Doublet of hol (“hallway, lobby”) and cela (“cell”).

parole.significato: improvisation (the act or art of composing and making music, poetry, and the like, extemporaneously)
parole.testo: From either German Improvisation or French improvisation, from Italian improvvisazione.

parole.significato: inclusion (an addition or the act of including)
parole.testo: From either English inclusion or French inclusion, from Latin inclusio, inclusionis.

parole.significato: cavity (depression in the ground, either spontaneously or artificially created)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish jama. Sense 3 is a semantic loan from Latin cavum.

parole.significato: hawk (bird of prey belonging to the subfamily Accipitrinae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish jastrząb. Noun 2 sense 1 is a semantic loan from English hawk.
Borrowed from English juror, from Middle English jurour, jurrour, from Anglo-Norman jurour, from Old French jureor, from the verb jurer (“to swear”), or possibly from Latin iūrātor, iūrātōrem.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps borrowed from Slovak kapravý or from Ukrainian капра́вий (kaprávyj), ultimately from dialectal Proto-Slavic *kapra.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain, perhaps from Old East Slavic kap(ъ)turъ (kap(ŭ)turŭ), from Tatar kapturga, or from Lithuanian gobtuvas, from gobti.
From either Russian казарма (kazarma) or German Kaserne, ultimately from Italian caserma.

parole.significato: class (group, collection, category or set sharing characteristics or attributes)
parole.testo: Internationalism; possibly borrowed from German Klasse or French classe, ultimately from Latin classis. Noun sense 13 is a semantic loan from English class. First attested in 1688.
Possibly from dialectal Czech klavý, alternatively introduced into Polish by Roma from Slovak kľavý (“numb, rigid, torpid”) with a semantic shift. Compare Russian клёвый (kljóvyj).

parole.significato: any plant of the genus Caltha
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps a back-formation from *knietek, from Old Polish knietki, from Middle High German knotchen. Alternatively related to Proto-Slavic *gnětiti (“to kindle”).
From either English conversion or French conversion, from Latin conversiō.

parole.significato: landscape (portion of territory which the eye can comprehend in a single view)
parole.testo: From kraj + obraz. Calque of German Landschaft or French paysage. Coined by Joachim Lelewel.

parole.significato: king (male monarch; a man who heads a monarchy)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish król. Noun 2 sense 2, noun 2 sense 3, and noun 2 sense 4 and are an internationalism semantic loan; compare English king, French roi and German König. Doublet of Karol.

parole.significato: jacket (piece of clothing worn on the upper body outside a shirt or blouse, often waist length to thigh length)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps borrowed from Middle High German kapp-rock (“hooded coat”). Alternatively from Turkish kubur (“case”) + -ak. If so, doublet of kabura (“holster”).
Either deverbal from lakierować or from English lacquer, from French lacque, from Portuguese laca, lacca, from Persian لاک (lâk), from Hindi लाख (lākh), from Sanskrit लाक्षा (lākṣā).
Borrowed from Portuguese lambada or Spanish lambada. First attested in 1990.
Either from French malcontent, from Middle French malcontent, or from Italian malcontento.
Inherited from Old Polish minister. Noun 1 sense 1 is a semantic loan from French ministre.

parole.significato: minute (unit of time equal to sixty seconds)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish minuta. Sense 1 is a semantic loan from French minute or German Minute. Doublet of menu.

parole.significato: international (of or having to do with more than one nation)
parole.testo: From między- + narodowy. Internationalism calque of various European languages; compare English international, French international, German international. First attested in 1859. Cognates Lechitic cognates include Kashubian midzënôrodny and Silesian miyndzynarodowy. Further Slavic cognates include B
Inherited from Old Polish mnich. Noun 2 sense 1 is a semantic loan from German Mönch.
From mąż + -yna. Calque of Latin virago and Hebrew אשה. Coined by Jakub Wujek.

Inherited from Old Polish odpowiedni. By surface analysis, odpowiedzieć + -ni. Sense 1 is a semantic loan from Russian соотве́тствующий (sootvétstvujuščij), German entsprechend, or French correspondant. Cognate with Czech odpovědný.
Inherited from Old Polish obrzym. Noun 2 sense 2 is a semantic loan from English giant.

parole.significato: to open (to make the inside of something accessible or allow for passage by moving from a shut position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish otworzyć. Sense 7 is a semantic loan from English open.

parole.significato: hand puppet, glove puppet (type of puppet designed to be worn on the hand like a glove)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps borrowed from German Patsche + -yna + -ka. Alternatively, from earlier *palcynka, from palec (“finger”). Etymology 1 sense 3 is a semantic loan from English sock puppet.

parole.significato: pipette (small glass tube used for transferring liquid)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pipe or Italian pipa.

parole.significato: plan (a set of intended actions, usually mutually related, through which one expects to achieve a goal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plan. Sense 1 is a semantic loan from English plan and German Plan. First attested in the 19th century.

parole.significato: train (mechanical (traditionally steam-powered, now typically diesel or electrical) vehicle carrying a large number of…
parole.testo: Deverbal from pociągać. Sense 1 is a semantic loan from French train, English train, and German Zug. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from French inclination. First attested in 1550.

From podstawa + -owy. Sense 1, sense 2, sense 3, sense 4 and sense 5 are semantic loans from English basic or basal, French fondamental, German grundlegend, and Russian основно́й (osnovnój). First attested in 1808.
Inherited from Old Polish prasa. Sense 1 is a semantic loan from German Presse and French presse.

parole.significato: design (plan for the structure and functions of an artifact, building or system)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Projekt. First attested in 1656–1688. Sense 5 is a semantic loan from English project.

parole.significato: representative (one who represents someone or something)
parole.testo: From przedstawić + -ciel. Calque of French représentant or German Vertreter. First attested in 1820. Compare Czech představitel and Russian представи́тель (predstavítelʹ).

parole.significato: chance, accident; coincidence (situation which occurred that could not have been predicted)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish przypadek. Noun 1 sense 2, noun 1 sense 3, noun 1 sense 4 and noun 2 sense 1 are semantic loans from Latin cāsus, which displaced spadek. By surface analysis, przypadać + -ek. Compare Czech případek, Kashubian przëpôdk, and Russian припа́док (pripádok). Further compare Hung

parole.significato: rightness, righteousness; fairness (that what is right, fair, or in accordance with reality)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ratiō. Noun sense 6 is a semantic loan from German Ration. First attested in 1548. Doublet of rezon (“self-confidence”). Compare Silesian racyjŏ.

Inherited from Old Polish radziecki. By surface analysis, radca + -cki. Sense 1 is a semantic loan from Russian сове́тский (sovétskij). Displaced sowiecki as that was considered a derogatory word. Compare Ukrainian радя́нський (radjánsʹkyj).
Possibly borrowed from French retardation, or a learned borrowing from Latin retardātiō. First attested in 1606–1608.

Borrowed from French romance, from Spanish romance, itself probably a borrowing from either Old French romanz or Old Occitan romans, from Vulgar Latin rōmānicē, from Latin rōmānicus. Doublet of romansz.

parole.significato: sewer, street gutter (prepared channel in a surface)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish rynsztok, from German Rinnstein or from uncommon Rinnstock. While the latter does exist (despite the claims of some sources), it seems restricted to eastern German dialects, such as German Silesian, and is indeed first attested in M.A. Troc’s Polish-German dictionary of 174

parole.significato: net (device made from mesh, used for catching fish, butterflies, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish sieć. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English web. Sense 4 is a semantic loan from English network.
Borrowed from French spectateur, or a learned borrowing from Latin spectātor. First attested in the first half of the 17th century.

parole.significato: cooperative, co-op, collective (any co-operative, including housing, retail, utility, agricultural, banking, or worker…
parole.testo: From spółdziałać + -nia. Internationalism calque of various European languages; compare English cooperative, French coopérative, German Kooperative, ultimately from Latin cooperātīvus. First attested in 1921.

parole.significato: state (a condition; a set of circumstances applying at any given time)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish stan. Sense 1, sense 2 and sense 2.1 are semantic loans from Latin status.
Possibly from Proto-Slavic *sъtъkъ. Etymology 2 sense 2 is a semantic loan from Latin cloāca.

parole.significato: relation, relationship (manner in which two things may be associated)
parole.testo: From stosować + -unek. Sense 7 and sense 6 are semantic loans from English relations. Sense 8 is a semantic loan from English connections and contacts. Sense 9 is a semantic loan from English terms. First attested in 1781. Cognate with English stotting.

parole.significato: side; face (one of two faces of a sheet of paper; or, the content thereon)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish strona. Sense 11 is a semantic loan from Latin genus verbī, English voice, and German Diathese, and sense 3 is a semantic loan from English website, web page, German Webseite, French page, and Russian ве́б-страни́ца (véb-straníca).

Uncertain. * Doroszewski suggests an association with English shoplifting. * Bańko suggests that the word may have either derived from German Schuppen or Yiddish שאָפּע (shope) which later, due to the massive migration of Jewish diaspora to the United States in the last XIX century, may have overlap

parole.significato: terrace, fluvial terrace (step-like landform, often in a river valley)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French terrasse or German Terrasse. Doublet of taras.

parole.significato: term; date (time set aside to do something, defined as a certain period or as a specific day)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin terminus (“boundary, limit, end”). Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English term and French terme. First attested in the 16th century. Compare Silesian termin and Slovincian termyn.
Inherited from Old Polish towarzysz. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from Russian това́рищ (továrišč).
Borrowed from Spanish tilde, from Latin titulus (“superscript”) or from tildar. Doublet of tytuł (“title”).

parole.significato: pointer (breed of dog used for finding game)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish wyżeł, from Proto-Slavic *vyžьlъ. By surface analysis, wyga + -eł. Alternatively borrowed from Hungarian vizsla, itself probably a borrowing from Slavic. Cognate to Czech vyžle, Russian выжла (vyžla) and Serbo-Croatian vižao/Serbo-Croatian вижао.
Borrowed from German Zunder. Alternatively, a common Slavic word, cognate with Czech sádra, Old Church Slavonic сядра (sjadra) and Serbo-Croatian седра, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sendʰro-.

parole.significato: wall (each of the substantial structures acting either as the exterior of or divisions within a structure)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish ściana. Sense 9 is a semantic loan from English wall.

parole.significato: snow (frozen, crystalline state of water that falls as precipitation)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish śnieg. Sense 3 is a semantic loan from English snow.
Borrowed from Belarusian жы́чка (žýčka) or Ukrainian жічка /жи́чка (žička).

parole.significato: trough (elongated container located in a stable or barn into which animal food is placed)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish żłób. Etymology 1, noun 2 sense 1 is a semantic loan from Yiddish זשלאָב (zhlob, “redneck, bumpkin”). Doublet of żleb (“couloir”), a borrowing from Slovak.
